questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q32
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: A superspeedway in New Delhi has among the highest super-elevation rates of any track on the Indian Grand Prix circuit. The track requires drivers to negotiate turns with a radius of 335 m and 33° banking. Given this information, the coefficient of side friction required in order to allow a vehicle to travel at 320 km/h along the curve is:
questions.explanation:
Highway Engineering | Geometric Design

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Radius of curve, \(R = 335\) m
    • Banking angle, \(\theta = 33^\circ\)
    • Design velocity, \(V = 320\) km/h
  • Aim: Determine the coefficient of side friction (\(f\)) required.

3. Core Concepts:

Super-elevation Equation: The general equation balancing centrifugal force against the components of weight and lateral friction is:\[e + f = \frac{v^2}{gR} \]where:
\(e = \tan\theta\) (Super-elevation rate or tangent of the banking angle)
\(f\) = Coefficient of lateral/side friction
\(v\) = velocity in m/s
\(g\) = acceleration due to gravity (\(\approx 9.81\) m/s²)
\(R\) = radius in meters

4. Solution Method:

  1. Convert the velocity \(V\) from km/h to m/s.
  2. Calculate the super-elevation \(e\) from the given angle \(\theta\).
  3. Substitute the values into the formula to solve for \(f\).

Pitfall Warning: Avoid arbitrarily using the simplified formula \(\dfrac{V^2}{225R}\) which is for design mixed traffic conditions. This is a racing track, so the exact equilibrium formula \(v^2/gR\) applies.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Unit Conversions\[v = 320 \times \frac{5}{18} = 88.889 \text{ m/s} \]\[e = \tan(33^\circ) = 0.6494 \]

Step 2: Calculate specific centrifugal ratio\[\frac{v^2}{gR} = \frac{(88.889)^2}{9.81 \times 335} = \frac{7901.25}{3286.35} = 2.404 \]

Step 3: Solve for side friction\[e + f = 2.404 \]\[f = 2.404 - 0.6494 = 1.755 \]Note: Option (A) is 1.761. If intermediate velocity is rounded to \(89\) m/s, then \(89^2 / (9.81 \times 335) - \tan(33^\circ) = 1.761\). This rounding quirk is a known trait of this specific exam question. The closest analytical answer is definitively Option A.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 1.761  |  Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q33
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question:
The following statements are made related to the lengths of turning lanes at signalised intersections:

(i)    1.5 times the average number of vehicles (by vehicle type) that would store in turning lane per cycle during the peak hour
(ii)    2 times the average number of vehicles (by vehicle type) that would store in turning lane per cycle during the peak hour
(iii)    Average number of vehicles (by vehicle type) that would store in the adjacent through lane per cycle during the peak hour
(iv)    Average number of vehicles (by vehicle type) that would store in all lanes per cycle during the peak hour

As per the IRC recommendations, the correct choice for design length of storage lanes is:
questions.explanation:
Highway Engineering | Traffic Engineering

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall / Comprehension
  • Given Data: Four statements defining methodologies for calculating the length of turning (storage) lanes.
  • Aim: Identify the correct IRC recommendation for the design length of storage lanes.

3. Core Concepts:

IRC Guidelines for Signalised Intersections (IRC:93 / IRC SP:41): Storage lanes for turning vehicles must accommodate the maximum queue generated to avoid spilling over and obstructing the adjacent through lane.

  • Provision 1 (Statement i): To account for the random arrival of vehicles (Poisson distribution of traffic), the lane length is determined based on 1.5 to 2.0 times the average number of vehicles storing in the turning lane per cycle during the peak hour.
  • Provision 2 (Statement iii): The queue length in the turning lane should not be less than the queue forming in the adjacent through lane. If the through-lane queue is longer, it will block access to the turning lane, rendering it useless.
  • Design Rule: The length must satisfy both constraints. Therefore, the design length must be the maximum of the two values.

4. Solution Method:

Evaluate the statements against IRC standards:

  • (i) is a valid IRC parameter (1.5 times the turning vehicles). ✓
  • (iii) is the secondary limiting constraint (adjacent through lane queue). ✓
  • The final design length must safely accommodate the worst-case scenario, choosing the maximum value between (i) and (iii).

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: Maximum of (i and iii)  |  Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q34
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question: In a leveling work, sum of the Back Sight (B.S.) and Fore Sight (F.S.) have been found to be 3.085 m and 5.645 m respectively. If the Reduced Level (R.L.) of the starting station is 100.000 m, the R.L. (in m) of the last station is _____________.
questions.explanation:
Geomatics Engineering | Surveying (Levelling)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Sum of Back Sights, \(\sum \text{B.S.} = 3.085\) m
    • Sum of Fore Sights, \(\sum \text{F.S.} = 5.645\) m
    • Reduced Level of First Station, \(\text{R.L.}_{\text{first}} = 100.000\) m
  • Aim: Calculate the Reduced Level (R.L.) of the last station.

3. Core Concepts:

Principle of Levelling Check: Irrespective of the method used (Height of Instrument or Rise and Fall), the arithmetic check for levelling states that the difference between the sum of Back Sights and the sum of Fore Sights strictly equals the difference in elevation between the last and first points.\[\text{R.L.}_{\text{last}} - \text{R.L.}_{\text{first}} = \sum \text{B.S.} - \sum \text{F.S.} \]

4. Solution Method:

Rearrange the basic levelling equation to isolate the unknown (\(\text{R.L.}_{\text{last}}\)) and plug in the given sums.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Isolate the unknown\[\text{R.L.}_{\text{last}} = \text{R.L.}_{\text{first}} + \sum \text{B.S.} - \sum \text{F.S.} \]

Step 2: Substitute values and calculate\[\text{R.L.}_{\text{last}} = 100.000 + 3.085 - 5.645 \]\[\text{R.L.}_{\text{last}} = 100.000 - 2.560 = 97.440 \text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 97.44 m  |  Accepted key range: 97.44 to 97.44

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q35
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question: The combined correction due to curvature and refraction (in m) for a distance of 1 km on the surface of Earth is:
questions.explanation:
Geomatics Engineering | Surveying Corrections

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Distance of sight, \(d = 1\) km
  • Aim: Determine the magnitude of the combined correction due to curvature and refraction in meters.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Curvature Correction (\(C_c\)): The earth's curvature makes the object appear lower than it actually is. It is always subtractive (−).\[C_c \approx -0.0785\, d^2 \quad (d \text{ in km, } C_c \text{ in m}) \]
  • Refraction Correction (\(C_r\)): Atmospheric refraction bends the line of sight downward, making the object appear higher. It is always additive (+).\[C_r \approx +0.0112\, d^2 \quad (d \text{ in km, } C_r \text{ in m}) \]
  • Combined Correction (\(C\)): The net mathematical sum of curvature and refraction.\[C = C_c + C_r = -0.0785\, d^2 + 0.0112\, d^2 = -0.0673\, d^2 \]Note: Magnitudes are usually presented as positive in surveying multiple choice options unless signs are specifically requested.

4. Solution Method:

Substitute the distance \(d = 1\) km directly into the empirical combined correction formula to extract the magnitude.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Apply formula\[|C| = 0.0673 \times d^2 = 0.0673 \times (1)^2 = 0.0673 \text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.0673 m  |  Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q36
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question:
The probability density function of a random variable, \(x\) is
\[f(x) = \dfrac{x}{4}(4 - x^2) \quad \text{for} \quad 0 \le x \le 2 \]
\[= 0 \quad \text{otherwise} \]
The mean, \(\mu_x\) of the random variable is _____________.
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Probability & Statistics

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Probability density function (PDF): \(f(x) = \dfrac{x}{4}(4 - x^2)\) for \(0 \le x \le 2\)
    • \(f(x) = 0\) otherwise
  • Aim: Calculate the mean, \(\mu_x\), of the random variable \(x\).

3. Core Concepts:

Expectation (Mean) of a Continuous Random Variable: The expected value or mean \(\mu_x\) of a continuous random variable having a probability density function \(f(x)\) is given by the integral over its entire domain:\[ \mu_x = E[x] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x \cdot f(x)\, dx \]

Properties of PDF: The total area under the PDF curve must equal 1 (verification step).

4. Solution Method:

  1. Setup the expected value integral using the given piecewise PDF bounds.
  2. Expand the polynomial term \(x \cdot f(x)\) inside the integral.
  3. Integrate term-by-step using the power rule.
  4. Evaluate the definite integral over the bounds \(x = 0\) to \(x = 2\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Set up the integral
The bounds where \(f(x) \neq 0\) are from \(0\) to \(2\).\[ \mu_x = \int_{0}^{2} x \cdot \left[\frac{x}{4}(4 - x^2)\right] dx \]

Step 2: Expand the integrand\[\mu_x = \int_{0}^{2} \frac{x^2}{4}(4 - x^2)\, dx = \frac{1}{4}\int_{0}^{2}(4x^2 - x^4)\, dx \]

Step 3: Integrate using the power rule \(\left(\int x^n\, dx = \dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}\right)\)\[ \mu_x = \frac{1}{4}\left[\frac{4x^3}{3} - \frac{x^5}{5}\right]_{0}^{2} \]

Step 4: Apply the limits of integration\[ \mu_x = \frac{1}{4}\left[\frac{4(8)}{3} - \frac{32}{5}\right] = \frac{1}{4}\left[\frac{32}{3} - \frac{32}{5}\right] \]

Step 5: Simplify to final fraction\[ \mu_x = \frac{32}{4}\left[\frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{5}\right] = 8\left[\frac{5-3}{15}\right] = 8 \times \frac{2}{15} = \frac{16}{15} \approx 1.0667 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 1.067  |  Accepted key range: 1.06 to 1.07

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q37
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question:
Consider the following second order linear differential equation
\[\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = -12x^2 + 24x - 20 \]
The boundary conditions are: at \(x = 0, y = 5\) and at \(x = 2, y = 21\)
The value of \(y\) at \(x = 1\) is _____________.
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Differential Equations

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Differential Equation: \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = -12x^2 + 24x - 20\)
    • Boundary Condition 1: \(y = 5\) at \(x = 0\)
    • Boundary Condition 2: \(y = 21\) at \(x = 2\)
  • Aim: Evaluate the value of the function \(y\) at \(x = 1\).

3. Core Concepts:

Successive Integration: A second-order ordinary differential equation (ODE) of the form \(y'' = f(x)\) can be solved by integrating \(f(x)\) twice.

Boundary Value Problem: Each integration introduces an arbitrary constant (\(C_1, C_2\)). Boundary conditions are used to solve for these constants to find the exact particular solution.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Integrate the given second derivative once to find the slope equation \(dy/dx\), adding constant \(C_1\).
  2. Integrate \(dy/dx\) to find the general equation for \(y(x)\), adding constant \(C_2\).
  3. Substitute \(x=0,\, y=5\) to directly solve for \(C_2\).
  4. Substitute \(x=2,\, y=21\) to solve for \(C_1\).
  5. Evaluate the fully resolved particular equation \(y(x)\) at \(x=1\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: First Integration\[\frac{dy}{dx} = \int(-12x^2 + 24x - 20)\, dx = -4x^3 + 12x^2 - 20x + C_1 \]

Step 2: Second Integration\[y(x) = \int(-4x^3 + 12x^2 - 20x + C_1)\, dx = -x^4 + 4x^3 - 10x^2 + C_1 x + C_2 \]

Step 3: Apply Boundary Condition 1
At \(x = 0,\, y = 5\):\[5 = 0 + 0 - 0 + 0 + C_2 \implies C_2 = 5 \]

Step 4: Apply Boundary Condition 2
At \(x = 2,\, y = 21\):\[21 = -(2)^4 + 4(2)^3 - 10(2)^2 + 2C_1 + 5 \]\[21 = -16 + 32 - 40 + 2C_1 + 5 \implies 21 = -19 + 2C_1 \implies C_1 = 20 \]Equation becomes: \(y(x) = -x^4 + 4x^3 - 10x^2 + 20x + 5\)

Step 5: Evaluate at \(x = 1\)\[y(1) = -1 + 4 - 10 + 20 + 5 = 18 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 18  |  Accepted key range: 18

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q38
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question: The two Eigen values of the matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & p \end{bmatrix}\) have a ratio of 3:1 for \(p = 2\). What is another value of \(p\) for which the Eigen values have the same ratio of 3:1?
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Linear Algebra

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Matrix \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & p \end{bmatrix}\)
    • For \(p = 2\), eigenvalues ratio is 3:1
  • Aim: Find another scalar value of \(p\) maintaining the exact same eigenvalue ratio of 3:1.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Trace of a Matrix: Sum of main diagonal elements = Sum of eigenvalues: \(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = \text{Tr}(A)\).
  • Determinant of a Matrix: Determinant = Product of eigenvalues: \(\lambda_1 \cdot \lambda_2 = \text{Det}(A)\).
  • Eigenvalue Ratio: If the ratio is \(3:1\), one eigenvalue is triple the other, i.e., \(\lambda_1 = 3\lambda_2\).

4. Solution Method:

  1. Express sum and product of eigenvalues in terms of \(p\) using Trace and Determinant properties.
  2. Substitute \(\lambda_1 = 3\lambda_2\) to form a system of equations.
  3. Eliminate \(\lambda_2\) to create a quadratic equation entirely in terms of \(p\).
  4. Solve the quadratic equation to find both values of \(p\). Select the "other" root.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Set up trace and determinant\[\text{Trace} = \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = 2 + p \]\[\text{Determinant} = \lambda_1 \cdot \lambda_2 = 2p - 1 \]

Step 2: Incorporate eigenvalue ratio
Let the eigenvalues be \(3\lambda\) and \(\lambda\).\[\text{Sum: } 4\lambda = p + 2 \implies \lambda = \frac{p+2}{4} \]\[\text{Product: } 3\lambda^2 = 2p - 1 \]

Step 3: Substitute \(\lambda\) into the product equation\[3\left(\frac{p+2}{4}\right)^2 = 2p - 1 \]\[3(p^2 + 4p + 4) = 16(2p - 1) \]\[3p^2 + 12p + 12 = 32p - 16 \]

Step 4: Solve the quadratic equation\[3p^2 - 20p + 28 = 0 \]\[p = \frac{20 \pm \sqrt{400 - 336}}{6} = \frac{20 \pm \sqrt{64}}{6} = \frac{20 \pm 8}{6} \]Root 1: \(p = \dfrac{28}{6} = \dfrac{14}{3}\)
Root 2: \(p = \dfrac{12}{6} = 2\) (given in problem)

The "other" value for \(p\) is \(\dfrac{14}{3}\).

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(\dfrac{14}{3}\)  |  Correct option: (D)

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q39
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question:
For step-size, \(\Delta x = 0.4\), the value of following integral using Simpson’s 1/3 rule is _____________.
\[\int_{0}^{0.8} (0.2 + 25x - 200x^2 + 675x^3 - 900x^4 + 400x^5) dx \]
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Numerical Methods

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Integral: \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{0.8} f(x)\, dx\)
    • \(f(x) = 0.2 + 25x - 200x^2 + 675x^3 - 900x^4 + 400x^5\)
    • Step-size, \(\Delta x = 0.4\)
  • Aim: Evaluate the integral numerically using Simpson's 1/3 rule.

3. Core Concepts:

Simpson's 1/3 Rule Formula: For an interval divided into two segments of equal width \(h = \Delta x\),\[ I \approx \frac{h}{3}\left[y_0 + 4y_1 + y_2\right] \]where \(y_0, y_1, y_2\) are function values evaluated at nodal coordinates \(x_0, x_1, x_2\).

4. Solution Method:

  1. Determine the coordinate points (\(x_0, x_1, x_2\)) spanning the domain \([0, 0.8]\) based on \(h = 0.4\).
  2. Calculate exact function values at each nodal point.
  3. Apply Simpson's 1/3 summation formula.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Identify nodal coordinates\[x_0 = 0, \quad x_1 = 0.4, \quad x_2 = 0.8 \]

Step 2: Evaluate \(f(x)\) at each node
For \(x_0 = 0\): \(y_0 = f(0) = 0.2\)

For \(x_1 = 0.4\):\[y_1 = 0.2 + 25(0.4) - 200(0.16) + 675(0.064) - 900(0.0256) + 400(0.01024) \]\[y_1 = 0.2 + 10 - 32 + 43.2 - 23.04 + 4.096 = 2.456 \]For \(x_2 = 0.8\):\[y_2 = 0.2 + 25(0.8) - 200(0.64) + 675(0.512) - 900(0.4096) + 400(0.32768) \]\[y_2 = 0.2 + 20 - 128 + 345.6 - 368.64 + 131.072 = 0.232 \]

Step 3: Apply Simpson's 1/3 Rule\[ I = \frac{0.4}{3}\left[y_0 + 4y_1 + y_2\right] = \frac{0.4}{3}\left[0.2 + 4(2.456) + 0.232\right] \]\[ I = \frac{0.4}{3}\left[0.2 + 9.824 + 0.232\right] = \frac{0.4}{3} \times 10.256 = \frac{4.1024}{3} \approx 1.367 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 1.37  |  Accepted key range: 1.36 to 1.37

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q40
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: In a system, two connected rigid bars \(AC\) and \(BC\) are of identical length, \(L\) with pin supports at \(A\) and \(B\). The bars are interconnected at \(C\) by a frictionless hinge. The rotation of the hinge is restrained by a rotational spring of stiffness, \(k\). The system initially assumes a straight line configuration, \(ACB\). Assuming both the bars as weightless, the rotation at supports, \(A\) and \(B\), due to a transverse load, \(P\) applied at \(C\) is:
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Energy Methods & Kinematics

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Two rigid bars AC and BC, each of length \(L\).
    • Pin supports at A and B.
    • Center hinge C with rotational spring, stiffness \(k\).
    • Point load \(P\) applied transversely at C.
  • Aim: Find the rotation \(\theta\) at supports A and B.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Kinematics of Rigid Bars: If point C undergoes a small transverse displacement \(\Delta\), the rotation of each bar at the pins A and B is geometrically defined as \(\theta = \dfrac{\Delta}{L}\).
  • Relative Rotation: The total "kinking" angle at the hinge C is the sum of the rotations of the two bars, so \(\alpha = \theta_A + \theta_B = 2\theta\).
  • Principle of Virtual Work / Energy Conservation: External work done by the force \(P\) exactly equals the internal strain energy stored in the rotational spring.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Express structural deflections in terms of \(\theta\).
  2. State the equation for Work Done (\(W\)).
  3. State the equation for Strain Energy (\(U\)).
  4. Equate \(W = U\) and solve directly for \(\theta\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Formulate Geometry
Let support rotations be \(\theta\).
Central displacement: \(\Delta = L\theta\).
Relative angle at hinge C: \(\alpha = \theta - (-\theta) = 2\theta\).

Step 2: External Work Done
For a slowly applied linear load:\[W = \frac{1}{2}P \cdot \Delta = \frac{1}{2}P(L\theta) \]

Step 3: Internal Strain Energy
Energy stored in a rotational spring is \(\dfrac{1}{2}k(\text{angle})^2\):\[U = \frac{1}{2}k\alpha^2 = \frac{1}{2}k(2\theta)^2 = 2k\theta^2 \]

Step 4: Equate Energy\[U = W \implies 2k\theta^2 = \frac{1}{2}PL\theta \]Dividing both sides by \(\theta\) (assuming \(\theta \neq 0\)):\[2k\theta = \frac{1}{2}PL \implies \theta = \frac{PL}{4k} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(\dfrac{PL}{4k}\)  |  Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q41
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: A simply supported reinforced concrete beam of length 10 m sags while undergoing shrinkage. Assuming a uniform curvature of 0.004 m⁻¹ along the span, the maximum deflection (in m) of the beam at mid-span is _____________.
questions.explanation:
Solid Mechanics | Deflection of Beams

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Simply supported RC beam span, \(L = 10\) m.
    • Undergoes shrinkage causing uniform curvature, \(\kappa = 0.004\) m\(^{-1}\).
  • Aim: Calculate maximum central deflection (\(\delta\)) in meters.

3. Core Concepts:

Moment-Curvature Relationship: Uniform curvature (\(\kappa\)) means the beam deforms into an arc of a circle. Small-deflection theory defines curvature as \(\kappa = \dfrac{1}{R} = -\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\).

Standard Case Deflection: For a simply supported beam subjected to uniform curvature across its whole length (similar to a uniform bending moment profile), the maximum midspan deflection mathematically maps to:\[\delta_{max} = \frac{\kappa L^2}{8} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Formulate the differential equation for deflection \(y'' = -\kappa\).
  2. Integrate twice to find the general deflection profile \(y(x)\).
  3. Use simply supported boundary conditions (\(y(0) = 0,\, y(L) = 0\)) to locate maximum deflection at \(x = L/2\).
  4. Plug given values into the derived formula.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Derived Formula Recall
From \(y'' = -\kappa\):\[y(x) = \frac{\kappa x}{2}(L - x) \]At midspan \(x = L/2\):\[\delta_{max} = \frac{\kappa(L/2)}{2}\left(L - \frac{L}{2}\right) = \frac{\kappa L}{4} \cdot \frac{L}{2} = \frac{\kappa L^2}{8} \]

Step 2: Plug in values
\(\kappa = 0.004\) m\(^{-1}\), \(L = 10\) m

Step 3: Compute final deflection\[\delta_{max} = \frac{0.004 \times (10)^2}{8} = \frac{0.4}{8} = 0.05 \text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.05 m  |  Accepted key range: 0.05 to 0.05

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q42
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: A steel strip of length, \(L = 200\) mm is fixed at end \(A\) and rests at \(B\) on a vertical spring of stiffness, \(k = 2\) N/mm. The steel strip is 5 mm wide and 10 mm thick. A vertical load, \(P = 50\) N is applied at \(B\), as shown in the figure. Considering \(E = 200\) GPa, the force (in N) developed in the spring is _____________.
questions.explanation:
Solid Mechanics | Deflection & Compatibility

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Fixed-free steel cantilever beam length, \(L = 200\) mm.
    • Rests on a vertical spring at the free end, stiffness \(k_s = 2\) N/mm.
    • Strip cross-section: Width \(b = 5\) mm, Depth \(d = 10\) mm.
    • Modulus of Elasticity, \(E = 200\) GPa.
    • Vertical load applied at free end, \(P = 50\) N.
  • Aim: Calculate the internal compressive force developed in the vertical spring.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Flexural Rigidity (\(EI\)): Derived from section properties. \(I = \dfrac{bd^3}{12}\) for a rectangular section bent about its horizontal axis.
  • Equivalent Stiffness (\(k_b\)): A cantilever subject to a point load at its free end acts like a spring with stiffness \(k_b = \dfrac{3EI}{L^3}\).
  • Parallel Spring Concept: Because both the beam and the vertical spring deflect exactly the same amount \(\Delta\) under the applied load \(P\), they act as springs in parallel.
  • Compatibility: \(P = k_b\Delta + k_s\Delta = (k_b + k_s)\Delta\).

4. Solution Method:

  1. Convert all parameters to consistent N and mm units.
  2. Calculate the area moment of inertia \(I\).
  3. Compute the structural stiffness of the cantilever \(k_b\).
  4. Determine global deflection \(\Delta\) using combined stiffness.
  5. Evaluate spring force via Hooke's Law: \(F_s = k_s \cdot \Delta\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Unit Conversion & Section Properties\[E = 200 \text{ GPa} = 200{,}000 \text{ N/mm}^2 \]\[I = \frac{5 \times 10^3}{12} = \frac{5000}{12} = 416.667 \text{ mm}^4 \]\[EI = 200{,}000 \times 416.667 = 83.333 \times 10^6 \text{ N·mm}^2 \]

Step 2: Cantilever Stiffness\[k_b = \frac{3EI}{L^3} = \frac{3 \times 83.333 \times 10^6}{200^3} = \frac{250 \times 10^6}{8{,}000{,}000} = 31.25 \text{ N/mm} \]

Step 3: Deflection Calculation\[P = (k_b + k_s)\Delta \implies 50 = (31.25 + 2)\Delta = 33.25\,\Delta \]\[\Delta = \frac{50}{33.25} \text{ mm} \]

Step 4: Spring Force\[F_s = k_s \cdot \Delta = 2 \times \frac{50}{33.25} = \frac{100}{33.25} \approx 3.008 \text{ N} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 3.01 N  |  Accepted key range: 3.0 to 3.3

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q43
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: A simply supported beam AB of span, \(L = 24\) m is subjected to two wheel loads acting at a distance, \(d = 5\) m apart as shown in the figure below. Each wheel transmits a load, \(P = 3\) kN and may occupy any position along the beam. If the beam is an I-section having section modulus, \(S = 16.2\) cm³, the maximum bending stress (in GPa) due to the wheel loads is _____________.
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Influence Lines & Moving Loads

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Simply supported span, \(L = 24\) m.
    • Two moving wheel loads, \(P_1 = P_2 = 3\) kN.
    • Distance between loads, \(d = 5\) m.
    • Beam section modulus, \(S = 16.2\) cm³ \(= 16.2 \times 10^{-6}\) m³.
  • Aim: Calculate the maximum bending stress generated in the beam in GPa.

3. Core Concepts:

Maximum Bending Moment under Moving Loads: For a system of two equal moving point loads on a simply supported beam, the absolute maximum bending moment occurs underneath one of the loads when the center of the beam's span is positioned perfectly midway between that load and the resultant center of gravity (CG) of the entire load system.

Formula for Max Moment:\[M_{max} = \frac{2P}{L}\left(\frac{L}{2} - \frac{d}{4}\right)^2 \]

Flexure Formula: \(\sigma = \dfrac{M_{max}}{S}\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Determine absolute maximum moment by applying the specific formula.
  2. Convert the max bending moment units properly.
  3. Compute maximum stress utilizing the given section modulus.
  4. Scale result to Gigapascals (GPa) as requested.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Calculate Absolute Maximum Bending Moment (\(M_{max}\))
The resultant of two equal loads \(3\) kN is \(6\) kN, acting exactly in the middle between them (i.e., at \(d/2 = 2.5\) m from each load). Max moment occurs under one load when the span center bisects the distance between that load and the resultant (\(d/4 = 1.25\) m from center).\[M_{max} = \frac{2(3)}{24}\left(\frac{24}{2} - \frac{5}{4}\right)^2 = \frac{6}{24}(12 - 1.25)^2 \]\[M_{max} = 0.25 \times (10.75)^2 = 0.25 \times 115.5625 = 28.891 \text{ kN·m} \]

Step 2: Convert Units\[M_{max} = 28.891 \times 10^3 \text{ N·m}, \quad S = 16.2 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^3 \]

Step 3: Calculate Bending Stress\[\sigma = \frac{M_{max}}{S} = \frac{28.891 \times 10^3}{16.2 \times 10^{-6}} = 1.7834 \times 10^9 \text{ Pa} \]

Step 4: Convert to GPa\[\sigma = 1.783 \text{ GPa} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 1.783 GPa  |  Accepted key range: 1.78 to 1.79

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q44
questions.subject: Concrete & Steel Structures
questions.topic: Limit State Design of Beams & Slabs
questions.question: According to the concept of Limit State Design as per IS 456: 2000, the probability of failure of a structure is _____________.
questions.explanation:
Structural Engineering | Limit State Design

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data: Limit State Design concept as per IS 456:2000.
  • Aim: Determine the theoretical probability of failure of a structure.

3. Core Concepts:

In Limit State Design (probabilistic approach), both the material strength and the loads are assumed to follow a normal distribution curve.

  • Characteristic Strength (\(f_{ck}\)): The strength below which not more than 5% of the test results are expected to fall. Thus, the probability of actual strength being less than characteristic strength is \(P_S = 0.05\).
  • Characteristic Load (\(L_c\)): The load which has a 95% probability of not being exceeded during the life of the structure. Thus, the probability of the actual load exceeding the characteristic load is \(P_L = 0.05\).

For a structure to be definitively safe, two independent events must happen simultaneously: (1) the load must be less than the characteristic load, and (2) the material strength must be greater than the characteristic strength.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Probability of safety concerning load \(= 1 - P_L = 1 - 0.05 = 0.95\)
  2. Probability of safety concerning strength \(= 1 - P_S = 1 - 0.05 = 0.95\)
  3. Overall probability of safety \(= 0.95 \times 0.95 = 0.9025\)
  4. Theoretical probability of failure:\[P_f = 1 - 0.9025 = 0.0975 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.0975  |  Accepted key range: 0.09 to 0.10

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q45
questions.subject: Concrete & Steel Structures
questions.topic: Limit State Design of Beams & Slabs
questions.question: In a pre-stressed concrete beam section shown in the figure, the net loss is 10% and the final pre-stressing force applied at \(X\) is 750 kN. The initial fiber stresses (in N/mm²) at the top and bottom of the beam were:
questions.explanation:
Structural Engineering | Prestressed Concrete

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Cross-section: \(b = 250\) mm, Total depth \(D = 200 + 200 = 400\) mm.
    • Final prestressing force applied at X: \(P_f = 750\) kN.
    • Distance of X from bottom fiber: \(d_2 = 100\) mm.
    • Net loss of prestress \(= 10\%\).
  • Aim: Initial fiber stresses at the top and bottom of the beam.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Centroid and Eccentricity: The centroidal axis passes through the mid-depth (\(y = D/2 = 200\) mm from top/bottom). The force is applied at 100 mm from the bottom, so its eccentricity \(e = 200 - 100 = 100\) mm below the neutral axis.
  • Initial Force: Since losses are 10%, the final force is 90% of the initial force: \(P_f = 0.9\, P_i\).
  • Combined Stresses: Stresses at any fiber are the sum of direct axial stress (\(P/A\)) and bending stress (\(M/Z\)). Compressive stresses are taken as positive.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Initial Prestressing Force (\(P_i\)):\[P_i = \frac{P_f}{0.9} = \frac{750}{0.9} = 833.333 \text{ kN} = 833.333 \times 10^3 \text{ N} \]
  2. Section Properties:\[A = 250 \times 400 = 100{,}000 \text{ mm}^2 \]\[Z = \frac{bD^2}{6} = \frac{250 \times 400^2}{6} = 6.667 \times 10^6 \text{ mm}^3 \]
  3. Stresses due to Initial Prestress:\[\sigma_d = \frac{P_i}{A} = \frac{833.333 \times 10^3}{100{,}000} = 8.333 \text{ MPa} \]\[M = P_i \times e = 833.333 \times 10^3 \times 100 = 83.333 \times 10^6 \text{ N·mm} \]\[\sigma_b = \frac{M}{Z} = \frac{83.333 \times 10^6}{6.667 \times 10^6} = 12.50 \text{ MPa} \]
  4. Resultant Initial Fiber Stresses:
    Top fiber (force acts below centroid → tension at top):\[\sigma_{top} = \sigma_d - \sigma_b = 8.333 - 12.50 = -4.167 \text{ MPa (Tension)} \]Bottom fiber (force causes compression at bottom):\[\sigma_{bot} = \sigma_d + \sigma_b = 8.333 + 12.50 = 20.833 \text{ MPa (Compression)} \]

6. Final Answer:

Correct option: (D)

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q46
questions.subject: Concrete & Steel Structures
questions.topic: Steel Tension, Compression Members & Plastic Analysis
questions.question: A fixed end beam is subjected to a load, W at 1/3rd span from the left support as shown in the figure. The collapse load of the beam is:
questions.explanation:
Structural Engineering | Structural Analysis (Plastic Analysis)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Fixed beam of span \(L\) with point load \(W\) at \(L/3\) from left support \(X\).
    • Left half capacity (\(0\) to \(L/2\)): \(2M_P\)
    • Right half capacity (\(L/2\) to \(L\)): \(M_P\)
  • Aim: Determine the collapse load \(W_c\).

3. Core Concepts:

We must check the Kinematic method for the most critical collapse mechanism. Potential plastic hinge locations are at the supports (\(X, Z\)), under the load (\(C\)), and at the change of cross-section (\(Y\)).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Mechanism 1 (Hinges at X, C, Z):
Let displacement at \(C\) be \(\delta\).\[\theta_X = \frac{\delta}{L/3} = \frac{3\delta}{L}, \quad \theta_Z = \frac{\delta}{2L/3} = \frac{1.5\delta}{L} \]Hinge rotation at \(C = \theta_X + \theta_Z = \dfrac{4.5\delta}{L}\)
Internal Work (capacities \(2M_P\) at \(X\), \(2M_P\) at \(C\), \(M_P\) at \(Z\)):\[W_I = (2M_P)\frac{3\delta}{L} + (2M_P)\frac{4.5\delta}{L} + (M_P)\frac{1.5\delta}{L} = 16.5\frac{M_P\delta}{L} \]External Work: \(W_E = W\delta \implies W_c = 16.5\dfrac{M_P}{L}\)

Mechanism 2 (Hinges at X, Y, Z):
Due to the abrupt reduction in capacity at \(Y\) (midspan), a hinge forms at \(Y\) instead of under the load. Let displacement at \(Y\) be \(\Delta\).\[\theta_X = \frac{\Delta}{L/2} = \frac{2\Delta}{L}, \quad \theta_Z = \frac{2\Delta}{L}, \quad \text{Hinge rotation at } Y = \frac{4\Delta}{L} \]Internal Work (capacities \(2M_P\) at \(X\), \(M_P\) at \(Y\), \(M_P\) at \(Z\)):\[W_I = (2M_P)\frac{2\Delta}{L} + (M_P)\frac{4\Delta}{L} + (M_P)\frac{2\Delta}{L} = 10\frac{M_P\Delta}{L} \]Displacement at \(C\) (by similar triangles) \(= \dfrac{L/3}{L/2}\Delta = \dfrac{2\Delta}{3}\)\[W_E = W\left(\frac{2\Delta}{3}\right) \]Equating:\[W\left(\frac{2\Delta}{3}\right) = 10\frac{M_P\Delta}{L} \implies W_c = 15.0\frac{M_P}{L} \]Validation: The bending moment at \(C\) for Mechanism 2 is \(1.667M_P\), well below its local capacity of \(2M_P\). Yield conditions are satisfied. Mechanism 2 gives the lower (critical) collapse load.

6. Final Answer:

Correct option: (C)  \(W_c = 15.0\,M_P/L\)

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q47
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: A 588 cm³ volume of moist sand weighs 1010 gm. Its dry weight is 918 gm and specific gravity of solids, G is 2.67. Assuming density of water as 1 gm/cm³, the void ratio is _____________.
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Soil Mechanics

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Total volume: \(V = 588\) cm³
    • Moist weight: \(W_{moist} = 1010\) gm
    • Dry weight of solids: \(W_s = 918\) gm
    • Specific gravity: \(G = 2.67\)
    • \(\rho_w = 1\) gm/cm³
  • Aim: Void ratio \(e\).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Dry Density: \(\gamma_d = \dfrac{W_s}{V}\)
  • Void Ratio Relationship: \(\gamma_d = \dfrac{G \cdot \gamma_w}{1 + e}\)

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Compute the dry density:\[\gamma_d = \frac{918}{588} = 1.5612 \text{ gm/cm}^3 \]
  2. Substitute into the specific gravity–void ratio relationship:\[1.5612 = \frac{2.67 \times 1.0}{1 + e} \implies 1 + e = \frac{2.67}{1.5612} = 1.7102 \]
  3. Solve for void ratio:\[e = 1.7102 - 1 = 0.7102 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.71  |  Accepted key range: 0.70 to 0.72

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q48
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: A 4 m thick layer of normally consolidated clay has an average void ratio of 1.30. Its compression index is 0.6 and coefficient of consolidation is 1 m²/yr. If the increase in vertical pressure due to foundation load on the clay layer is equal to the existing effective overburden pressure, the change in the thickness of the clay layer is _____________ mm
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Consolidation

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Clay thickness: \(H_0 = 4000\) mm
    • Initial void ratio: \(e_0 = 1.30\)
    • Compression index: \(C_c = 0.6\)
    • Added pressure equals existing effective overburden pressure: \(\Delta\sigma' = \sigma'_0\)
  • Aim: Change in thickness \(\Delta H\) in mm.

3. Core Concepts:

Primary consolidation settlement equation for Normally Consolidated (NC) clay:\[\Delta H = H_0 \left(\frac{C_c}{1 + e_0}\right) \log_{10}\left(\frac{\sigma'_0 + \Delta\sigma'}{\sigma'_0}\right) \]

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Evaluate the stress ratio term:
    Since \(\Delta\sigma' = \sigma'_0\), final stress \(\sigma'_f = 2\sigma'_0\).\[\frac{\sigma'_f}{\sigma'_0} = 2 \]
  2. Compute the settlement:\[\Delta H = 4000 \times \left(\frac{0.6}{1 + 1.30}\right) \times \log_{10}(2) \]\[\Delta H = 4000 \times \frac{0.6}{2.3} \times 0.30103 \]\[\Delta H = 1043.478 \times 0.30103 = 314.12 \text{ mm} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 314.12 mm  |  Accepted key range: 313.0 to 316.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q49
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: A pile of diameter 0.4 m is fully embedded in a clay stratum having 5 layers, each 5 m thick as shown in the figure below. Assume a constant unit weight of soil as 18 kN/m³ for all the layers. Using λ-method (λ = 0.15 for 25 m embedment length) and neglecting the end bearing component, the ultimate pile capacity (in kN) is _____________.
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Foundation Engineering (Pile Capacity)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Pile diameter: \(D = 0.4\) m
    • Fully embedded length: \(L = 25\) m in 5 clay layers of 5 m each.
    • Unit weight: \(\gamma = 18\) kN/m³ throughout.
    • \(c_u\) array: 40, 50, 60, 70, 80 kPa (layer by layer).
    • \(\lambda = 0.15\). Neglect end bearing.
  • Aim: Ultimate pile capacity using the \(\lambda\)-method.

3. Core Concepts:

According to Vijayvergiya and Focht's \(\lambda\)-method, the average unit skin friction is:\[f_{av} = \lambda(\bar{\sigma}'_v + 2\bar{c}_u) \]where \(\bar{\sigma}'_v\) is the mean effective vertical stress and \(\bar{c}_u\) is the mean undrained shear strength.
Pile capacity: \(Q_u \approx Q_s = f_{av} \times (\pi \cdot D \cdot L)\)

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Mean Effective Vertical Stress (\(\bar{\sigma}'_v\)):
    Stress at surface \(= 0\). Stress at bottom \(= 18 \times 25 = 450\) kPa.\[\bar{\sigma}'_v = \frac{0 + 450}{2} = 225 \text{ kPa} \]
  2. Mean Undrained Shear Strength (\(\bar{c}_u\)):\[\bar{c}_u = \frac{40 + 50 + 60 + 70 + 80}{5} = 60 \text{ kPa} \]
  3. Average Unit Skin Friction (\(f_{av}\)):\[f_{av} = 0.15 \times (225 + 2 \times 60) = 0.15 \times 345 = 51.75 \text{ kPa} \]
  4. Ultimate Capacity (\(Q_u\)):\[Q_u = 51.75 \times \pi \times 0.4 \times 25 = 51.75 \times 10\pi = 1625.77 \text{ kN} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 1625.77 kN  |  Accepted key range: 1620.0 to 1630.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q50
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: Stress path equation for tri-axial test upon application of deviatoric stress is, \(q = 10\sqrt{3} + 0.5 p\). The respective values of cohesion, c (in kPa) and angle of internal friction, φ are:
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Shear Strength

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Equation for stress path: \(q = 10\sqrt{3} + 0.5p\)
  • Aim: Find cohesion (\(c\)) and angle of internal friction (\(\phi\)).

3. Core Concepts:

In triaxial compression stress paths, the geometric parameters \((p, q)\) relate to Mohr-Coulomb parameters \((c, \phi)\) via:\[p = \frac{\sigma_1 + \sigma_3}{2}, \quad q = \frac{\sigma_1 - \sigma_3}{2} \]The failure envelope in the \(p\)-\(q\) plane is expressed as:\[q = p\sin\phi + c\cos\phi \]

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Compare \(q = 0.5p + 10\sqrt{3}\) with the standard equation \(q = p\sin\phi + c\cos\phi\).
  2. Angle of Internal Friction (\(\phi\)):\[\sin\phi = 0.5 \implies \phi = \arcsin(0.5) = 30^\circ \]
  3. Cohesion (\(c\)):\[c\cos(30^\circ) = 10\sqrt{3} \]\[c \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 10\sqrt{3} \implies c = 20 \text{ kPa} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(c = 20\) kPa, \(\phi = 30^\circ\)  |  Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q51
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: A 6 m high retaining wall having a smooth vertical back face retains a layered horizontal backfill. Top 3 m thick layer of the backfill is sand having an angle of internal friction, φ = 30° while the bottom layer is 3 m thick clay with cohesion, c = 20 kPa. Assume unit weight for both sand and clay as 18 kN/m³. The total active earth pressure per unit length of the wall (in kN/m) is:
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Earth Pressure

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: 6 m retaining wall.
    • Top 3 m: Sand, \(\gamma = 18\) kN/m³, \(c = 0\), \(\phi = 30^\circ\).
    • Bottom 3 m: Clay, \(\gamma = 18\) kN/m³, \(c = 20\) kPa, \(\phi = 0^\circ\).
  • Aim: Total active earth pressure per unit length.

3. Core Concepts:

Active Earth Pressure Equation: \(p_a = K_a\sigma_v - 2c\sqrt{K_a}\)

Coefficient of Active Earth Pressure: \(K_a = \dfrac{1 - \sin\phi}{1 + \sin\phi}\)

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Top Sand Layer (0 to 3 m):\[K_{a1} = \frac{1 - \sin 30^\circ}{1 + \sin 30^\circ} = \frac{0.5}{1.5} = \frac{1}{3} \]\(p_a\) at top (\(z = 0\)): \(0\)
    \(p_a\) at bottom of sand (\(z = 3\) m): \(\dfrac{1}{3} \times 18 \times 3 = 18\) kPa\[P_1 = \frac{1}{2} \times 18 \times 3 = 27 \text{ kN/m} \]
  2. Bottom Clay Layer (3 to 6 m):\[\phi = 0^\circ \implies K_{a2} = 1 \]Overburden at \(z = 3\) m: \(\sigma_v = 18 \times 3 = 54\) kPa\[p_a \text{ at top of clay} = 1(54) - 2(20) = 14 \text{ kPa} \]Overburden at \(z = 6\) m: \(\sigma_v = 54 + 54 = 108\) kPa\[p_a \text{ at bottom of clay} = 1(108) - 2(20) = 68 \text{ kPa} \]\[P_2 = \frac{14 + 68}{2} \times 3 = 41 \times 3 = 123 \text{ kN/m} \]
  3. Total Force:\[P_{total} = P_1 + P_2 = 27 + 123 = 150 \text{ kN/m} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 150 kN/m  |  Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q52
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A field channel has cultivable commanded area of 2000 hectares. The intensities of irrigation for gram and wheat are 30% and 50% respectively. Gram has a kor period of 18 days, kor depth of 12 cm, while wheat has a kor period of 18 days and a kor depth of 15 cm. The discharge (in m³/s) required in the field channel to supply water to the commanded area during the kor period is _____________.
questions.explanation:
Water Resources Engineering | Irrigation Engineering

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: \(CCA = 2000\) ha.
    • Gram: Intensity \(30\%\), Kor period \(B_g = 18\) days, Kor depth \(\Delta_g = 0.12\) m.
    • Wheat: Intensity \(50\%\), Kor period \(B_w = 18\) days, Kor depth \(\Delta_w = 0.15\) m.
  • Aim: Required discharge \(Q\) in the field channel (m³/s).

3. Core Concepts:

Both crops are irrigated concurrently within their identically spaced 18-day Kor period. We must satisfy the combined volumetric demand.

  • Area for each crop: \(A = \text{CCA} \times \text{Intensity}\)
  • Continuous discharge formula: \(Q = \dfrac{A \times \Delta}{B\text{ (in seconds)}}\)

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Area to be Irrigated:\[A_{\text{gram}} = 2000 \times 0.30 = 600 \text{ ha} = 600 \times 10^4 \text{ m}^2 \]\[A_{\text{wheat}} = 2000 \times 0.50 = 1000 \text{ ha} = 1000 \times 10^4 \text{ m}^2 \]
  2. Determine Time in Seconds:\[T = 18 \times 24 \times 3600 = 1{,}555{,}200 \text{ s} \]
  3. Discharge for Gram (\(Q_g\)):\[Q_g = \frac{600 \times 10^4 \times 0.12}{1{,}555{,}200} = \frac{720{,}000}{1{,}555{,}200} = 0.4630 \text{ m}^3/\text{s} \]
  4. Discharge for Wheat (\(Q_w\)):\[Q_w = \frac{1000 \times 10^4 \times 0.15}{1{,}555{,}200} = \frac{1{,}500{,}000}{1{,}555{,}200} = 0.9645 \text{ m}^3/\text{s} \]
  5. Total Required Discharge:\[Q = Q_g + Q_w = 0.4630 + 0.9645 = 1.4275 \text{ m}^3/\text{s} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 1.43 m³/s  |  Accepted key range: 1.4 to 1.5

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q53
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A triangular gate with a base width of 2 m and a height of 1.5 m lies in a vertical plane. The top vertex of the gate is 1.5 m below the surface of a tank which contains oil of specific gravity 0.8. Considering the density of water and acceleration due to gravity to be 1000 kg/m³ and 9.81 m/s² respectively, the hydrostatic force (in kN) exerted by the oil on the gate is _____________.
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Hydrostatics

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Triangular gate: Base \(b = 2\) m, height \(h = 1.5\) m.
    • Submerged in oil (\(SG = 0.8\)).
    • Top vertex is \(1.5\) m below the free surface.
  • Aim: Hydrostatic force \(F\) exerted by the oil.

3. Core Concepts:

The total hydrostatic force on a vertical submerged plane surface is:\[F = \gamma_{oil} \cdot \bar{h} \cdot A \]where \(\gamma_{oil}\) is the specific weight of the oil, \(\bar{h}\) is the vertical depth to the centroid of the wetted area from the free surface, and \(A\) is the area of the triangular gate.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Specific Weight of Oil:\[\gamma_{oil} = SG \times \rho_w \times g = 0.8 \times 1000 \times 9.81 = 7848 \text{ N/m}^3 = 7.848 \text{ kN/m}^3 \]
  2. Depth of Centroid (\(\bar{h}\)):
    The gate has its vertex pointing up and horizontal base at bottom. The centroid of a triangle is \(2h/3\) from the vertex.\[\text{Distance of centroid from top vertex} = \frac{2}{3} \times 1.5 = 1.0 \text{ m} \]\[\bar{h} = 1.5 + 1.0 = 2.5 \text{ m} \]
  3. Area of Triangular Gate:\[A = \frac{1}{2} \times b \times h = \frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 1.5 = 1.5 \text{ m}^2 \]
  4. Calculate Hydrostatic Force:\[F = 7.848 \times 2.5 \times 1.5 = 29.43 \text{ kN} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 29.43 kN  |  Accepted key range: 29.3 to 29.5

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q54
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
The velocity components of a two dimensional plane motion of a fluid are: \(u = \dfrac{y^3}{3} + 2x - x^2y\) and \(v = xy^2 - 2y - \dfrac{x^3}{3}\).
The correct statement is:
options: Fluid is incompressible and flow is irrotational
Fluid is incompressible and flow is rotational
Fluid is compressible and flow is irrotational
Fluid is compressible and flow is rotational

structuredOptions.label: A
structuredOptions.text: Fluid is incompressible and flow is irrotational
structuredOptions.html: Fluid is incompressible and flow is irrotational

structuredOptions.label: B
structuredOptions.text: Fluid is incompressible and flow is rotational
structuredOptions.html: Fluid is incompressible and flow is rotational

structuredOptions.label: C
structuredOptions.text: Fluid is compressible and flow is irrotational
structuredOptions.html: Fluid is compressible and flow is irrotational

structuredOptions.label: D
structuredOptions.text: Fluid is compressible and flow is rotational
structuredOptions.html: Fluid is compressible and flow is rotational

questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Kinematics of Fluid Flow

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Velocity component in \(x\)-direction: \(u = \dfrac{y^3}{3} + 2x - x^2y\)
    • Velocity component in \(y\)-direction: \(v = xy^2 - 2y - \dfrac{x^3}{3}\)
  • Aim: Determine if the fluid is compressible or incompressible, and if the flow is rotational or irrotational.

3. Core Concepts:

Continuity Equation for 2D Incompressible Flow: A flow field is incompressible if the divergence of the velocity vector is zero.\[\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} = 0 \]

Rotationality (Vorticity): A 2D flow is irrotational if the spin (vorticity) about the \(z\)-axis is zero.\[\omega_z = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right) = 0 \]

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Check for Compressibility\[\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = 2 - 2xy, \quad \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} = 2xy - 2 \]\[\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} = (2 - 2xy) + (2xy - 2) = 0 \]Continuity equation is satisfied ⟹ fluid is incompressible.

Step 2: Check for Rotationality\[\frac{\partial v}{\partial x} = y^2 - x^2, \quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = y^2 - x^2 \]\[\frac{\partial v}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = (y^2 - x^2) - (y^2 - x^2) = 0 \]Vorticity is zero ⟹ flow is irrotational.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: Fluid is incompressible and flow is irrotational  |  Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q55
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: The average surface area of a reservoir in the month of June is 20 km². In the same month, the average rate of inflow is 10 m³/s, outflow rate is 15 m³/s, monthly rainfall is 10 cm, monthly seepage loss is 1.8 cm and the storage change is 16 million m³. The evaporation (in cm) in that month is:
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Water Balance

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Area: \(A = 20\) km² \(= 20 \times 10^6\) m²
    • Average Inflow rate: \(I = 10\) m³/s
    • Average Outflow rate: \(O = 15\) m³/s
    • Rainfall: \(P = 10\) cm \(= 0.1\) m
    • Seepage loss: \(S_L = 1.8\) cm \(= 0.018\) m
    • Absolute Storage change: \(|\Delta S| = 16\) million m³
    • Time period: June \(= 30\) days
  • Aim: Calculate Evaporation (\(E\)) in cm for that month.

3. Core Concepts:

Hydrological Water Budget Equation:\[(V_{\text{in}} + V_{\text{precip}}) - (V_{\text{out}} + V_{\text{seepage}} + V_{\text{evap}}) = \pm\Delta S \]Note: To ascertain whether \(\Delta S\) is \(+16\) or \(-16\), one performs a trial balance. An overall net deficit indicates \(\Delta S = -16\) Mm³.

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Calculate total volumes over 30 days (in Mm³)\[t = 30 \times 24 \times 3600 = 2.592 \times 10^6 \text{ s} \]

  • \(V_{\text{in}} = 10 \times 2.592 \times 10^6 = 25.92\) Mm³
  • \(V_{\text{out}} = 15 \times 2.592 \times 10^6 = 38.88\) Mm³
  • \(V_{\text{precip}} = 20 \times 10^6 \times 0.1 = 2.0\) Mm³
  • \(V_{\text{seepage}} = 20 \times 10^6 \times 0.018 = 0.36\) Mm³

Step 2: Apply the Water Budget Equation
Assuming storage reduction (\(\Delta S = -16\) Mm³) because outflow dramatically exceeds inflow:\[(25.92 + 2.0) - (38.88 + 0.36 + V_{\text{evap}}) = -16 \]\[27.92 - 39.24 - V_{\text{evap}} = -16 \implies V_{\text{evap}} = 16 - 11.32 = 4.68 \text{ Mm}^3 \](If \(\Delta S = +16\) were assumed, \(V_{\text{evap}}\) would be negative — confirming \(\Delta S\) must be negative.)

Step 3: Convert Evaporation Volume to Depth\[E = \frac{4.68 \times 10^6}{20 \times 10^6} = 0.234 \text{ m} = 23.4 \text{ cm} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 23.4 cm  |  Correct option: (D)

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q56
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A pipe of 0.7 m diameter has a length of 6 km and connects two reservoirs A and B. The water level in reservoir A is at an elevation 30 m above the water level in reservoir B. Halfway along the pipe line, there is a branch through which water can be supplied to a third reservoir C. The friction factor of the pipe is 0.024. The quantity of water discharged into reservoir C is 0.15 m³/s. Considering the acceleration due to gravity as 9.81 m/s² and neglecting minor losses, the discharge (in m³/s) into the reservoir B is _____________.
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Flow Through Pipes

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Pipe Diameter: \(D = 0.7\) m, Total Length: \(L = 6000\) m
    • Head difference: \(H = Z_A - Z_B = 30\) m
    • Midpoint branch at \(L_1 = 3000\) m, remaining \(L_2 = 3000\) m
    • Tap discharge at midpoint: \(Q_C = 0.15\) m³/s
    • Darcy friction factor: \(f = 0.024\)
    • \(g = 9.81\) m/s²
  • Aim: Find the discharge reaching reservoir B (\(Q_B\)).

3. Core Concepts:

Darcy-Weisbach Equation (in terms of Discharge):\[h_f = \frac{8fLQ^2}{\pi^2 g D^5} \]

Series Pipe System with a branch: Total head loss is the sum of losses in the two segments.\[H = h_{f1} + h_{f2} \]By continuity: \(Q_1 = Q_B + Q_C\) (first half), \(Q_2 = Q_B\) (second half).

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Formulate the head loss equation
Calculate the constant factor \(K\) for each segment (\(L_1 = L_2 = 3000\) m):\[K = \frac{8 \times 0.024 \times 3000}{\pi^2 \times 9.81 \times (0.7)^5} = \frac{576}{9.8696 \times 9.81 \times 0.16807} \approx 35.397 \text{ s}^2/\text{m}^5 \]\[ H = K\left[(Q_B + 0.15)^2 + Q_B^2\right] \]

Step 2: Setup quadratic equation\[ 30 = 35.397\left[(Q_B + 0.15)^2 + Q_B^2\right] \]\[0.8475 = 2Q_B^2 + 0.3Q_B + 0.0225 \]\[2Q_B^2 + 0.3Q_B - 0.825 = 0 \]

Step 3: Solve for \(Q_B\)\[Q_B = \frac{-0.3 \pm \sqrt{0.09 + 6.6}}{4} = \frac{-0.3 \pm \sqrt{6.69}}{4} = \frac{-0.3 \pm 2.5865}{4} \]Taking the positive root:\[Q_B = \frac{2.2865}{4} = 0.5716 \text{ m}^3/\text{s} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.571 m³/s  |  Accepted key range: 0.56 to 0.58

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q57

questions.question: A landfill is to be designed to serve a population of 200000 for a period of 25 years. The solid waste (SW) generation is 2 kg/person/day. The landfill volume (in million m³) required is _____________.

Environmental Engineering | Solid Waste Management

  • Given Data:

    • SW generation rate \(= 2\) kg/person/day
    • Un-compacted SW density \(= 100\) kg/m³
    • Compaction ratio \(= 4\)
    • Compacted fill (SW + cover) to compacted SW ratio \(= 1.5\)
  • Aim: Calculate required total landfill volume.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Mass of Solid Waste: \(M = \text{Population} \times \text{Rate} \times \text{Time}\)

Step 2: Volume of Un-compacted SW\[V_{\text{uncompacted}} = \frac{3.65 \times 10^9}{100} = 36.5 \times 10^6 \text{ m}^3 \]

questions.question: A water treatment plant of capacity, 1 m³/s has filter boxes of dimensions 6 m × 10 m. Loading rate to the filters is 120 m³/day/m². When two of the filters are out of service for back washing, the loading rate (in m³/day/m²) is _____________.

Environmental Engineering | Water Treatment

    • Filter box dimensions: \(6\) m \(\times\) \(10\) m \(= 60\) m² per filter
    • Design loading rate: \(120\) m³/day/m²
    • Number of filters out of service: \(2\)

3. Core Concepts:

  • Total design area required: \(A_{\text{total}} = \dfrac{Q}{\text{Design Loading Rate}}\)
  • Total number of filter units: \(N = \dfrac{A_{\text{total}}}{A_{\text{individual}}}\)
  • New Loading Rate: \(LR_{\text{new}} = \dfrac{Q}{(N-2) \times A_{\text{individual}}}\)

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Total initial filter area and number of filters\[A_{\text{total}} = \frac{86{,}400}{120} = 720 \text{ m}^2 \]\[N = \frac{720}{60} = 12 \text{ filters} \]

Step 2: New effective area after backwashing isolation
Operational filters \(= 12 - 2 = 10\)\[A_{\text{active}} = 10 \times 60 = 600 \text{ m}^2 \]

Step 3: Calculate new loading rate\[LR_{\text{new}} = \frac{86{,}400}{600} = 144 \text{ m}^3/\text{day/m}^2 \]

questions.question: The relation between speed \(u\) (in km/h) and density \(k\) (number of vehicles / km) for a traffic stream on a road is \(u = 70 - 0.7k\). The capacity on this road is _____________ vph (vehicles/hour).

Greenshield's Macroscopic Stream Model: Posits a linear speed-density relationship:\[u = u_f\left(1 - \frac{k}{k_j}\right) \]where \(u_f\) is Free Mean Speed and \(k_j\) is Jam Density.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 1750 vph  |  Accepted key range: 1750

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q63
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: In Marshall method of mix design, the coarse aggregate, fine aggregate, fines and bitumen having respective values of specific gravity 2.60, 2.70, 2.65 and 1.01, are mixed in the relative proportions (% by weight) of 55.0, 35.8, 3.7 and 5.5 respectively. The theoretical specific gravity of the mix and the effective specific gravity of the aggregates in the mix respectively are:
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Pavement Design

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: Proportions by weight (\(W_i\)) and specific gravities (\(G_i\)):
    ComponentWeight (%)Specific Gravity
    Coarse aggregate55.02.60
    Fine aggregate35.82.70
    Fines3.72.65
    Bitumen5.51.01
  • Aim: Calculate theoretical specific gravity of mix (\(G_t\)) and effective specific gravity of aggregates (\(G_{se}\)).

Theoretical Maximum Specific Gravity of Mix (\(G_t\)): Weighted harmonic mean of all constituents.\[G_t = \frac{100}{\sum\left(\dfrac{W_i}{G_i}\right)} \]

Effective Specific Gravity of Aggregate (\(G_{se}\)): Back-calculated from mix \(G_t\).\[G_{se} = \frac{100 - W_b}{\dfrac{100}{G_t} - \dfrac{W_b}{G_b}} \]Note: The rounded value of \(G_t\) is used to compute \(G_{se}\) as modeled by the test setter.

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q64

questions.question: The bearings of two inaccessible stations, \(S_1\) (Easting 500 m, Northing 500 m) and \(S_2\) (Easting 600 m, Northing 450 m) from a station \(S_3\) were observed as 225° and 153° 26' respectively. The independent Easting (in m) of station \(S_3\) is:
questions.explanation:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • \(S_1\) Coordinates: \((500, 500)\)
    • \(S_2\) Coordinates: \((600, 450)\)

Line bearing angles map to geometry using:\[\tan(\text{Bearing}) = \frac{E - E_3}{N - N_3} \]

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

questions.question: Two Pegs A and B were fixed on opposite banks of a 50 m wide river. The level was set up at A and the staff readings on Pegs A and B were observed as 1.350 m and 1.550 m, respectively. Thereafter the instrument was shifted and set up at B. The staff readings on Pegs B and A were observed as 0.750 m and 0.550 m, respectively. If the R.L. of Peg A is 100.200 m, the R.L. (in m) of Peg B is _____________.
questions.explanation:
Geomatics Engineering | Levelling

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    SetupStaff on A (m)Staff on B (m)
    At A\(a_1 = 1.350\)\(b_1 = 1.550\)
    At B\(a_2 = 0.550\)\(b_2 = 0.750\)
    Elevation (R.L.) of Peg A \(= 100.200\) m.
  • Aim: True Reduced Level (R.L.) of Peg B.

3. Core Concepts:

Reciprocal Levelling: Used to eliminate earth's curvature, refraction, and collimation errors. True elevation difference is the average of apparent elevation differences from both setups:\[\Delta h = \frac{(b_1 - a_1) + (b_2 - a_2)}{2} \]Sign Convention: If \(b > a\) consistently, point B lies physically lower than point A.

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Calculate apparent elevation differences

  • From Setup at A: \(b_1 - a_1 = 1.550 - 1.350 = 0.200\) m
  • From Setup at B: \(b_2 - a_2 = 0.750 - 0.550 = 0.200\) m

Step 2: Calculate true elevation difference\[\Delta h = \frac{0.200 + 0.200}{2} = 0.200 \text{ m} \]Since \(\Delta h > 0\), B is 0.200 m lower than A.

Step 3: Calculate R.L. of B\[\text{R.L. of } B = 100.200 - 0.200 = 100.000 \text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 100.000 m  |  Accepted key range: 100
